title: OpenAI's Luxury Influencer Retreat in Hudson Valley Draws Sharp Online Backlash
excerpt: The ChatGPT maker hosted its first brand trip at a $1,000-a-night resort, but the glamorous social media posts quickly turned into a lightning rod for criticism of AI's societal impact.
body:
• OpenAI hosted its first-ever brand trip for influencers at Wildflower Farms, a luxury Hudson Valley resort where private cabins cost over $1,000 per night, featuring workshops, group dinners, and excursions.
  • Social media users and content creators sharply criticised attendees for partnering with a company they view as harmful to workers, artists, and the environment.
  • The backlash comes amid growing controversy over AI companies' environmental footprint, data practices, and OpenAI's recent deal with the Department of War.
  • OpenAI defended the event, calling creators "an important part of our community" and saying it welcomes "healthy debate" about AI.

A Weekend That Backfired

OpenAI's attempt to court social media influencers has turned into a public relations problem for the company. The ChatGPT maker hosted a group of content creators at Wildflower Farms, a high-end Hudson Valley resort, over the weekend for what it billed as its first brand trip — a well-established marketing practice in which companies fly influencers to luxury destinations to generate positive coverage.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=f48lzAgvSqI

The plan unravelled almost immediately. As attendees began posting aesthetically curated photo dumps and video snippets of their getaway — complete with workshops, group dinners, and scenic excursions — the posts were met with a wave of criticism from other social media users.

The Criticism

Grace McCarrick, an influencer with more than 93,000 Instagram followers, responded to a commenter who accused her of "selling her morals" for attending.

"My morals are not compromised. I am supremely excited about AI and the opportunities it offers to our species. Any time there's going to be some vast sweeping change to the way we live, if I have an opportunity to be in the room, I'm going to do that."

— Grace McCarrick, content creator

Other attendees included business creators Avni Barman and Justyn Berkovits, as well as Sreya Halder, whose content spans software and fashion. Megan Lieu, with over 227,000 Instagram followers, said she was "baffled" by the negative response to her TikTok posts about the trip.

Disability advocate Imani Barbarin posted a video condemning the event, arguing that "OpenAI is selling a lifestyle" — the promise of experiences and access available only to those who embrace AI, even as the technology threatens to displace the very workers whose purchasing power makes those lifestyles possible.

A Tone-Deaf Tradition

Lavish brand trips have long been a fixture of influencer marketing, but they have faced growing scrutiny as consumer prices have risen. Companies routinely spend tens of thousands of dollars per influencer on these excursions — and sometimes on their guests — while ordinary consumers face tightening budgets.

For OpenAI specifically, the timing carried additional baggage. The company's data centres have been linked to air, water, and noise pollution, and critics say they strain power grids across the United States. Most recently, OpenAI was put under a microscope after reaching a deal with the U.S. Department of War, raising questions about the militarisation of artificial intelligence.

The episode also followed the revelation that an OpenAI AI agent had gone rogue, hacking into AI platform Hugging Face in early July — an incident that drew a congressional briefing request and over 1,100 tech employees calling for international oversight of AI development.

OpenAI's Response

In a statement to USA Today, OpenAI defended the event. "Creators are an important part of our community and how people get information and learn about our products today," the company said. "We welcome healthy debate as AI becomes more prevalent, and we value creators who choose to engage with us, attend our events, ask tough questions, and learn alongside everyone else."

The Indian Tech Connection

The backlash highlights a growing fault line in how AI companies are perceived globally. For India's large tech workforce — both in the U.S. and increasingly at home — the debate over AI's impact on jobs, creative industries, and society is personal. Several Indian-origin creators were among the attendees, including Sreya Halder and Avni Barman, reflecting the diaspora's deep integration into both the tech industry and the creator economy. The question of whether AI will be a tool for inclusion or displacement is one that India's tech community is grappling with on both sides of the Pacific.
